title: Nested Structs and Composition
learningObjectives: Access nested fields using chained dot operations.
Use composition to represent has-a relationships.
Avoid overly deep or confusing nested designs.

understand.concept: Composition places one object inside another as a member. The contained object is part of the containing object's lifetime.
understand.whyItMatters: Composition models real entities with components, such as address within customer.
understand.explain: Access nested members with chained dot operators and initialize components deliberately.

examples.title: Nested object
examples.code: struct Address{int zip;};\nstruct Person{Address address;};\nPerson p{{12345}};
examples.explanation: Address is a member of Person.

examples.title: Access nested member
examples.code: struct Date{int day;};\nstruct Event{Date date;};\nEvent e{{18}};std::cout<<e.date.day;

examples.title: Compose dimensions
examples.code: struct Size{int w;int h;};\nstruct Window{Size size;};\nWindow w{{800,600}};

examples.title: Initialize nested values
examples.code: struct Engine{int cc;};\nstruct Car{Engine engine;int year;};\nCar c{{1600},2020};
examples.explanation: Nested aggregates follow member declaration order.

examples.title: Composition access
examples.code: struct Battery{int percent;};\nstruct Device{Battery battery;};\nDevice d{{85}};d.battery.percent=90;
examples.explanation: Nested field can be updated through the parent.

practise.guidedTask: For Nested Structs and Composition, trace every example. List each type, object, member, initial value, access path, and state change. Identify where encapsulation or initialization affects correctness.
practise.independentTask: Create a small C++ model focused on Nested Structs and Composition (such as a Point, Student, Product, or Account). Include multiple objects, initialization, at least one operation/member access, and test normal, boundary and invalid states. Explain which fields should be public or private and why.
hints: Define the type and its responsibilities before creating objects.
Initialize members deliberately and trace their values.
Use dot for objects and arrow only for pointers.
Keep fields private when they must enforce rules.
Test object creation, valid operations and rejected updates.
